title: Latency Economics Planner: per-request phase-split & kernel-stitch policy
creator: Asha Patel
description: Problem: Current prefill/decode allocator uses static phase-split heuristics and a separate kernel-hint pipeline. This leads to suboptimal decisions for mixed workloads: short low-cost requests get over-scheduled into dense kernels and small slices, increasing latency tails; long generative requests are sometimes routed to conservative kernels increasing cost. Goal: Build a per-request "Latency Economics Planner" (LEP) that combines latency budget, tenant priority, real-time kernel-cost profiles, and attention-sparsity signals to compute a recommended phase split (prefill vs decode micro-slices), kernel preference (dense / sparse / quantized variant), and hedging/fallback policy. The planner should emit a compact decision blob consumed by the existing arbiter and kernel-selection layer. This ticket covers design, sim, and an initial canary rollout path.
acceptance_criteria: LEP produces deterministic decision blobs for given input features and weights
Simulated workloads show >=10% reduction in p95 latency for mixed short-heavy workloads versus baseline
No regression (>1%) in overall throughput for throughput-oriented tenants
Integration tests for kernel hinting and fallback paths pass in CI
Canary rollout to 5% of production traffic with metrics and rollback automation
design_decisions: Use a lightweight scoring model (linear combination + small decision tree) rather than an NN to keep decisions explainable and cheap

Decision inputs: tenant_priority, latency_budget_ms, token_length_est, attention_sparsity_score, recent_kernel_latency_estimate, recent_kernel_cost_estimate, tenant_credit, request_type (chat/generation/embedding)
Output: phase_split_percentiles (prefill vs decode micro-slices), preferred_kernel_tag, hedging_policy (percent fallback), slice_size_hint
Expose a tunable weight vector via remote config for quick experiments and rollback
Keep the planner stateless per-request; rely on telemetry push for updating kernel estimates
tradeoffs: Explainability vs optimality: simple model enables faster rollout and SRE signoff but may miss nuanced patterns captured by ML models
Centralized decision computation vs decentralized: single planner component simplifies tuning but adds an RPC hop; we mitigate with co-located planner instances on serving nodes
Fairness enforcement adds scheduling overhead and may slightly increase average latency for low-priority tenants to protect high-priority SLAs
Aggressive micro-slicing reduces p95 but increases scheduler overhead and kernel churn
implementation_plan: 1) Add feature extractor in request path to emit input vector and record to a short-lived request context
2) Implement LEP core as a Go service library with a config-driven weight table and unit tests
3) Add simulation harness extension to replay historical traces with LEP decisions and compute A/B metrics
4) Integrate decision blob into arbiter API; ensure backward compatibility (fall back to existing heuristics if missing)
5) End-to-end integration test (local) + perf test on a small GPU cluster
6) Canary rollout (5% -> 20% -> 50%) with automatic rollback on SLO regressions
7) Post-launch tuning and weight updates driven by measured cost/latency tradeoffs
test_plan: Unit tests for scoring logic and boundary conditions
Simulation tests using three trace classes: short-chat-heavy, long-sampling-heavy, mixed-multi-tenant
Load test with artificial attention-sparsity patterns to verify kernel demotion/promotion
Canary observability: p50/p95/p99 latency, tail amplification, throughput, cost-per-token, tenant fairness gap metric
Chaos test: simulate kernel-side slowdown to validate hedging and fallback behaviors
metrics: kernel-choice distribution (dense vs sparse vs quantized)
tenant-fairness-gap = max(p95_tenant) - min(p95_tenant) across active tenants
rate of fallbacks and hedged requests
dependencies: ENG-990122 (arbiter-decision-blobs) - API extension for decision consumption
INF-ops-alerting (dashboard templates) - canary dashboards and alert rules
